name: Fisetin
lead: Fisetin (3,3',4',7-tetrahydroxyflavone) is a plant flavonol in the polyphenol family. It occurs as a yellow pigment in fruits and vegetables such as strawberries, apples, persimmons, onions and cucumbers, and its chemical formula was first described by the Austrian chemist Josef Herzig in 1891.[1] It is sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement and is discussed in longevity communities as a candidate senolytic, a compound proposed to selectively clear senescent cells.[2][3]

Interest rose after a 2018 EBioMedicine paper reported that fisetin acted as a senotherapeutic that extended health and lifespan in mice.[4] Human data remain limited to small or early-phase trials, several of them registered but not yet reporting, and Wikipedia states that there was no clinical evidence of benefit to human health as of 2018.[1] No published human trial has tested fisetin for skin, hair or facial appearance outcomes.

Fisetin is a supplement and not an approved therapy for any condition. Research reviews describe its oral bioavailability as low, and efforts to improve absorption through new formulations are under way.[5][6]

paras: Fisetin is a flavonol with a 3-hydroxyflavone core; it differs from the related flavonol quercetin by lacking a hydroxyl group at the 5-position, which is why it is sometimes called 5-deoxyquercetin.[7] Grokipedia reports it was first isolated in 1833 from the smoke tree (Rhus cotinus), a source of yellow dye, and that it is found in plant families including Fabaceae, Moraceae and Anacardiaceae, with strawberries often cited as the richest common dietary source.[7] It is poorly soluble in water and sensitive to light and oxidation.[7] Review articles also discuss methods for preparing it at pharmaceutical quality.[8]

Fisetin shares the antioxidant properties of other polyphenols and has been reported in laboratory work to have anti-inflammatory, chemopreventive and neuroprotective activity.[8][9][10] Fisetin and quercetin were among the first agents identified as senolytics, drugs that make senescent cells susceptible to their own pro-apoptotic environment.[11][12] Senescent cells accumulate with age and secrete an inflammatory mixture called the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP); researchers in the field have proposed that clearing them intermittently, a so-called hit-and-run approach, could delay age-related conditions.[11][13]

A 2017 study in Aging reported fisetin alongside BCL-XL inhibitors as new agents targeting senescent cells.[12] Cell studies have also shown flavonoids, including fisetin, to inhibit phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase signalling.[14] Some work describes a dual character, with phenoxyl radicals of flavonoids having prooxidant activity under some conditions.[15]

Fisetin has low oral bioavailability. A 2022 randomised double-blind crossover study in healthy volunteers compared a novel hybrid-hydrogel formulation with unformulated fisetin and reported enhanced bioavailability for the formulated product.[6] Reviews of fisetin as a senotherapeutic say that safety, pharmacokinetics and efficacy still need to be established in humans.[5]

The senolytic hypothesis is supported mainly by cell and animal work. A review of senolytic drugs reports that in preclinical models they delay, prevent or alleviate frailty and diseases of many organ systems, with translation to humans only beginning.[11][13] A 2024 narrative review concluded that fisetin offers a promising strategy for multiple chronic diseases but stressed that more studies are required to establish safety, pharmacokinetics and efficacy.[5] A separate review of senotherapy in oncology lists fisetin with metformin, rapamycin, dasatinib, quercetin and others as agents that eliminate senescent cells in cell cultures and murine models.[16]

Other lab reports include protection against kidney fibrosis in mice via effects on ferroptosis,[17] a mitochondria-targeted fisetin derivative that limited survival of drug-induced senescent breast cancer cells,[18] and in vitro neuroprotection by quercetin-related flavonoids that was limited in vivo by blood-brain barrier passage for quercetin.[19]

Published randomised trials of fisetin are few and mostly outside the senescence field. A double-blind placebo-controlled trial in ischaemic stroke patients examined whether fisetin could extend the treatment window for tissue plasminogen activator.[20] A placebo-controlled, pseudo-randomised crossover trial tested botanical agents including fisetin (from Rhus succedanea) for Gulf War illness.[21] Two 2026 randomised trials in obese men combined fisetin supplementation with interval resistance-aerobic training and measured adipokines such as asprosin and inflammatory markers including Maresin-1.[22][23] The 2022 hybrid-hydrogel study above is a pharmacokinetic trial in healthy people.[6]

Registered trials target ageing biology. ClinicalTrials.gov lists studies of fisetin for reducing systemic senescence (n=82),[24] vascular function in older adults,[25][26] senescence and walking impairment in peripheral artery disease,[27] multimorbidity,[28] healthy ageing,[29] age-related lung decline,[30] carpal tunnel syndrome,[31] mild Alzheimer's disease,[32] and COVID-19 inflammation.[33] Grokipedia reports that Mayo Clinic's AFFIRM frailty trials had no peer-reviewed primary results posted as of late 2026.[7] No clinical studies on appearance outcomes were found.

Fisetin is generally regarded as low hazard in dietary contexts, though direct contact can irritate skin, eyes and airways.[7] Human safety data at the higher doses discussed in longevity communities are limited, and drug interactions have not been well characterised in published trials.[5]

Fisetin is sold as a supplement. On T Nation, contributors list it among mitochondrial and longevity compounds alongside urolithin A, NAD+ and PQQ,[34] mention strawberries as a fisetin source in discussions of dietary phytochemicals,[35] and have run articles calling it a potential next polyphenol supplement comparable to curcumin and attributing to it effects including reduced body fat, blood sugar regulation and UV skin protection in animal work.[36][37] No looksmax.org or Reddit discussion was identified.

timeline.event: Fisetin is reportedly first isolated from the smoke tree.[7]
Josef Herzig describes its chemical formula.[1]
Fisetin is reported as a new senolytic agent in Aging.[12]
A mouse study reports that fisetin extends health and lifespan.[4]
A human crossover study tests a hybrid-hydrogel fisetin formulation.[6]
A review evaluates fisetin as a senotherapeutic and cites early phase I/II trials.[5]

lore.intro: Fisetin is discussed mainly in longevity and supplement circles, including on T Nation, as a senolytic or polyphenol supplement; it is not a core looksmaxxing topic.[34][36]

claims.claim: Fisetin clears senescent cells and extends lifespan
claims.believers: Supporters point to mouse research reporting extended health and lifespan and to the senolytic literature that names fisetin among the first senolytic agents.[4][11]
claims.experts: The findings are from animal and cell studies; a 2024 review says safety, pharmacokinetics and efficacy still need to be established in humans, and Wikipedia states there was no clinical evidence of human benefit as of 2018.[1][5]

claims.claim: Fisetin supports mitochondrial repair and healthy ageing
claims.believers: A T Nation poster recommends it with urolithin A, NAD+ and PQQ for those interested in mitochondrial repair.[34]
claims.experts: Registered trials in older adults are testing vascular function, senescence and frailty, but no peer-reviewed primary efficacy results have been reported for the frailty trials.[7][25][24]

claims.claim: Fisetin reduces body fat, regulates blood sugar and protects skin from UV
claims.believers: A T Nation article lists these as reported benefits, along with extending lifespan in lab animals.[37]
claims.experts: Two 2026 randomised trials in obese men studied fisetin with training and measured adipokines and inflammatory markers, not appearance outcomes; no human trial has tested fisetin for UV skin protection.[22][23]

claims.claim: Dietary fisetin from strawberries is beneficial
claims.believers: A T Nation poster lists strawberries as a source of fisetin among healthy phytochemical-rich foods.[35]
claims.experts: Fisetin occurs in strawberries, apples and onions, but clinical benefit from dietary amounts has not been shown, and the low oral bioavailability of the pure compound is a recognised limitation.[1][6]
